title: B-Tree & B+Tree Indexes
summary: The default index in every relational database — how a balanced multi-way tree turns a table scan into a handful of page reads, and why B+Tree beat B-Tree for disk-backed storage.

slides.markdown:
When you run `CREATE INDEX` in Postgres, MySQL, or SQL Server without saying otherwise, you get a **B+Tree** — the default index structure almost everywhere. It's a balanced, multi-way tree tuned specifically for disk: shallow enough that a lookup on a billion-row table costs **3-4 page reads**, and it supports both exact-match and range queries from the same structure.

Understanding why it's shaped the way it is — wide and shallow, not narrow and deep like a binary tree — explains why indexes are fast, why some don't get used, and what "index height" means when a DBA talks about it.

slides.sectionTitle: Balanced multi-way tree: height vs fanout
slides.markdown:
A B+Tree is **balanced** — every leaf sits at the same depth — and **multi-way**, meaning each internal node holds many keys and many child pointers, not just two like a binary tree. That branching factor is the **fanout**.

With an 8 KB page, a 16-byte key (say a bigint id plus overhead), and an 8-byte child pointer, one node can hold roughly **8192 / 24 ≈ 340 entries** — a fanout in the hundreds. A tree with fanout 340 needs only **height 4** to index over **340^4 ≈ 13 billion** keys.

That's the whole trick: high fanout keeps height tiny, and height is what determines how many page reads a lookup costs. A binary tree indexing 13 billion keys would need height ~34 — 34 disk reads instead of 4.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a B+Tree with a leaf-level linked list
slides.markdown:
![A three-level B+Tree with leaf nodes linked left to right](assets/btree-leaf-linked-list.svg)

Internal nodes exist only to route a search — they hold separator keys and child pointers, no row data. **Leaf nodes** hold the actual keys and pointers to rows (or the rows themselves, in a clustered index), and are additionally linked to each other in sorted order.

That leaf-level linked list is what makes range scans cheap: after descending once to find the start of a range, the engine just walks the linked list forward — no need to re-descend the tree for each subsequent key.

assets.alt: A three-level B+Tree with leaf nodes linked left to right

slides.markdown:
For `WHERE age BETWEEN 25 AND 35`, the engine descends the tree once — height 3-4 reads — to find the leaf containing `25`, then walks the leaf-linked-list rightward, collecting matching keys until it passes `35`. Each subsequent leaf is one sequential-ish page read, not a fresh root-to-leaf descent.

This is precisely why B+Trees dominate over structures like plain hash indexes for range predicates: a hash index can find `age = 25` in O(1), but has no concept of "next key," so it cannot answer a range query at all without scanning everything.

The cost of a range scan is roughly: tree height (one-time) + number of matching leaf pages (proportional to result size) — which is why a highly selective range is cheap and a range matching half the table often isn't worth using the index over.

The names get used loosely, but the distinction is precise and matters for disk-backed engines.

| | B-Tree | B+Tree |
|---|---|---|
| Data location | Every node (internal + leaf) can hold row data | Only leaf nodes hold row data; internal nodes hold only keys for routing |
| Leaf links | No inherent leaf linked list | Leaves linked in sorted order |
| Range scans | Requires in-order traversal, can revisit internal nodes | Sequential leaf walk — simple and fast |
| Fanout per page | Lower — internal nodes "waste" space on data | Higher — internal nodes are pure keys, packing more per page |
| Real-world use | Rare in disk databases today | Postgres, MySQL InnoDB, Oracle, SQL Server default |

**How to decide:** you rarely choose this yourself — virtually every relational database ships B+Tree as `CREATE INDEX`'s default — but knowing *why* (higher fanout, cheap ordered range scans) is the actual interview signal, not the name.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: an index on a low-selectivity column
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "I added an index on `status`, so queries filtering on it will be fast."

**Why it's wrong:** if `status` only has 3 distinct values across 10 million rows (`active`, `pending`, `closed`), each value matches roughly 3.3 million rows — over 30% of the table. The planner estimates that using the index means jumping between the index and the heap for millions of scattered row lookups, which costs more total I/O than just reading the table sequentially — so it correctly **ignores the index** and does a full scan.

**Correct model:** an index pays off when it's **selective** — filtering down to a small fraction of rows. Low-cardinality columns like booleans or status enums are usually bad standalone index candidates; they work better as part of a composite index led by a more selective column, or filtered with a partial index for just the rare value you actually query (e.g. `WHERE status = 'pending'`).

slides.sectionTitle: Composite indexes and the left-prefix rule
slides.markdown:
A **composite index** on `(last_name, first_name)` sorts rows first by `last_name`, then by `first_name` within each `last_name`. It's really one B+Tree over a concatenated key, not two separate indexes.

The **left-prefix rule** follows directly from that ordering: the index can serve `WHERE last_name = 'Kim'` and `WHERE last_name = 'Kim' AND first_name = 'Ana'` efficiently, because both start by narrowing on the leading column. But `WHERE first_name = 'Ana'` alone can't use this index efficiently — knowing only `first_name` gives you no useful position in a tree sorted by `last_name` first, so it degrades to a full scan.

The practical rule of thumb: order composite index columns by putting equality-filtered, most-selective columns first, and any range-filtered column last (since a range on a middle column breaks the tree's usefulness for columns after it).

slides.sectionTitle: Numbers: why height 4 handles billions of rows
slides.markdown:
Worth being able to derive live: with fanout ~340 (from an 8 KB page and ~24-byte entries), height 1 indexes 340 keys, height 2 indexes 340² ≈ 115,600, height 3 indexes 340³ ≈ 39 million, and height 4 indexes 340⁴ ≈ 13.4 billion.

This is why interviewers ask "how many disk reads does an index lookup cost on a 100-million-row table" and expect "3, maybe 4" rather than "it depends on the data." It's also why the root and often the first internal level of a large index stay permanently cached in the buffer pool — a few hundred KB of root/near-root pages get reused by every single lookup, so in practice a warm index lookup often costs only **1 real disk read** for the leaf page.

The number that matters in an interview isn't the formula — it's knowing index lookups are near-constant-time in practice, dominated by whether the leaf page is cached.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: index maintenance cost on writes
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Indexes only help; there's no downside to adding more of them."

**Why it's wrong:** every `INSERT`, `UPDATE` of an indexed column, or `DELETE` has to update **every** index on that table, not just the heap. A table with 6 indexes means a single insert does 7 writes (1 heap + 6 index entries) instead of 1. Worse, an insert with a random key (like a UUID primary key) causes scattered writes across the tree rather than appending at the rightward edge, and can trigger a **page split** — a full page divides into two half-full pages, temporarily doubling space and generating extra I/O.

**Correct model:** every index is a standing tax on writes, paid on every mutation forever, in exchange for faster reads on that specific query pattern — which is why over-indexing a write-heavy table is a real and common production mistake, not just a theoretical concern.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: B+Tree lookup vs full table scan cost
slides.markdown:
| | B+Tree index lookup | Full table scan |
|---|---|---|
| Cost shape | O(log_fanout n) — height of tree, ~3-4 page reads | O(n) — every page in the table |
| Best for | Selective filters, point lookups, small ranges | Filters matching a large fraction of rows |
| I/O pattern | Mostly random (tree descent), sequential on leaf walk | Fully sequential — cheap per page |
| Crossover | Planner picks the index below roughly 5-15% selectivity, workload dependent | Planner picks a scan above that threshold |

**How to decide:** this crossover is exactly why the query planner sometimes "ignores" a perfectly good index — for a query matching 40% of a table, sequential full-table I/O genuinely beats millions of random index-then-heap lookups, even though the index exists and is healthy.

slides.sectionTitle: Snapshot recap: what "index height" tells you
slides.markdown:
Most engines expose index height directly — Postgres via `pg_stat_user_indexes` plan output, MySQL via `SHOW INDEX` cardinality stats feeding the optimizer. A healthy B+Tree on a large table sits at **height 3-5**; if you see height climbing well beyond what the row count predicts, it's a signal of bloat — often from many deletes leaving under-full pages that never got merged back together.

The senior-level move is treating index height as a health metric you can reason about from first principles (fanout and row count), not just a number a tool reports — so when it drifts, you know whether it's expected growth or a sign the index needs a rebuild (`REINDEX` in Postgres, `OPTIMIZE TABLE` in MySQL).
